description: Test your knowledge of PA H12 | Blood Groups & Transfusion Medicine.

cards.text: What are ABO blood group antigens chemically, and why are they clinically significant?
cards.answer: Oligosaccharide chains attached to glycoproteins and glycolipids on RBC surfaces. Clinically significant because foreign antigens trigger alloimmune responses, causing haemolysis if incompatible blood is transfused.

tip.tip: Sugar chains on RBC surface; foreign chains = immune attack

cards.answer: The plasma always contains antibodies against the ABO antigens that are absent from that person's own red cells. Example: Group A has anti-B; Group B has anti-A; Group O has both anti-A and anti-B.

tip.tip: You have antibodies AGAINST what you DON'T have on your cells

cards.text: Describe how the H gene and ABO gene products work together to create blood group antigens.
cards.answer: The H gene encodes fucosyltransferase, which creates H substance (precursor). The ABO gene then modifies H substance: A allele adds GalNAc → A antigen; B allele adds galactose → B antigen; O allele is non-functional, leaving H substance unconverted.

tip.tip: H is the foundation; A and B are the builders modifying it; O leaves it alone

cards.text: When do natural isohaemagglutinins appear and what triggers their development?
cards.answer: Around 3–6 months of age, stimulated by environmental antigens (gut flora, pollen, food) that share oligosaccharide structures with ABO antigens. They are IgM class and activate complement efficiently.

tip.tip: Babies get AB antibodies from food & environment—no transfusion needed

cards.text: Why is ABO incompatibility immediately catastrophic on first blood transfusion, unlike Rh incompatibility?
cards.answer: Natural isohaemagglutinins (IgM, complement-activating) already exist in the plasma without any prior exposure or sensitization. Rh incompatibility requires prior sensitization to develop immune antibodies.

tip.tip: ABO = ready-made disaster; Rh = disaster only after sensitization

cards.text: What is the inheritance pattern of ABO blood groups? Give the phenotypes from each genotype.
cards.answer: A and B alleles are codominant; O is recessive. AA or AO → Group A; BB or BO → Group B; AB → Group AB; OO → Group O.

tip.tip: A & B codominant (AB person has both); O recessive (needs two copies)

cards.text: What is the Bombay phenotype, and why is it a clinical trap?
cards.answer: Homozygous non-functional H gene prevents H substance formation, blocking all A and B antigen synthesis. Types as Group O routinely, but plasma contains anti-A + anti-B + anti-H (most potent antibody combination). Can only receive blood from other Bombay donors.

tip.tip: Bombay looks like O, but IS NOT—has dangerous triple antibody

cards.text: Complete the blood group table: What antigens and antibodies does each ABO group have?
cards.answer: Group A: A antigen + anti-B antibodies. Group B: B antigen + anti-A antibodies. Group AB: A & B antigens + no ABO antibodies. Group O: H antigen only + anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

tip.tip: AB = both antigens, no antibodies. O = no A/B antigens, both antibodies
